questions.stem: Group 16 of the periodic table (oxygen family) is also called:

options.option_text: Noble gases, the inert gas group

questions.explanation: CHALCOGENS (Greek 'chalkos' = ore + 'genes' = born) — most metal ores are oxides, sulphides (e.g., haematite Fe₂O₃, galena PbS, zinc blende ZnS, copper pyrites CuFeS₂). Members: O (oxygen), S (sulphur), Se (selenium), Te (tellurium), Po (polonium — radioactive). Distractor 1: Group 17 = HALOGENS (salt-formers — F, Cl, Br, I). Distractor 3: Group 15 = PNICTOGENS (suffocators — N, P, As). Distractor 4: Group 18 = noble gases.

questions.stem: OZONE (O₃) in the upper atmosphere is important because it:

options.option_text: Absorbs harmful UV radiation from Sun
Causes the rain on planet Earth
Makes the sky appear blue colour

questions.explanation: OZONE LAYER (stratosphere, 15-35 km altitude): absorbs ~97-99% of Sun's UV-B + UV-C radiation → protects life from skin cancer, cataracts, plant damage. Discovered to have a 'hole' over Antarctica (1985, Farman et al.), caused by CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons in refrigerants, aerosols). MONTREAL PROTOCOL (1987) — international treaty to phase out CFCs; ozone layer recovering. World Ozone Day = 16 September. Distractor 1 — adds, but its function isn't supplemental O₂. Distractor 4 = Rayleigh scattering.

questions.stem: SULPHURIC ACID (H₂SO₄, 'King of Chemicals') is industrially produced by:

options.option_text: Ostwald process for nitric acid output

questions.explanation: CONTACT PROCESS: S + O₂ → SO₂; 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ (V₂O₅ catalyst, 450°C); SO₃ + H₂SO₄ → H₂S₂O₇ (oleum); oleum + H₂O → 2H₂SO₄. (Direct SO₃ + H₂O is too vigorous — uses oleum.) H₂SO₄ called 'KING OF CHEMICALS' — produced/consumed in vast quantities; an indicator of industrialisation. Uses: fertilizers (~60% — single super phosphate, ammonium sulphate), batteries (lead-acid), petroleum refining, dyes, drugs, detergents. India: Hazira, IFFCO produce it.

questions.stem: Sulphur exists in several allotropes. The MOST COMMON allotrope at room temperature is:

options.option_text: Hot liquid sulphur, S_n chains form

questions.explanation: RHOMBIC SULPHUR (α-sulphur) — stable at < 96°C; yellow octahedral crystals; S₈ rings (puckered crown shape). Most common allotrope. MONOCLINIC SULPHUR (β-sulphur) — stable 96-119°C; long needle-like crystals. PLASTIC SULPHUR — formed when molten S is cooled rapidly; rubbery, S∞ chains; unstable, reverts to rhombic. S has many S-atom oligomers: S₂, S₃, S₆, S₇... S₁₂. Sulphur sublimes at ~445°C with characteristic blue flame. Found native in volcanic regions, oil/gas (recovered as Claus process by-product).

questions.stem: Which gas, released by burning sulphur-containing fuel, is the main contributor to ACID RAIN?
questions.explanation: ACID RAIN: SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃ (sulphurous acid); 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃; SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄ (sulphuric acid). Also NOx (from vehicles, lightning) → HNO₃. pH of acid rain < 5.6 (normal rain pH ~5.6 due to CO₂). Damages: forests, lakes (kills fish), buildings (corrodes marble — Taj Mahal yellowing), soils. Sources: coal-burning power plants (high-S coal), smelters, vehicles. Solutions: scrubbers (FGD), low-S fuels, catalytic converters. Distractor 1 — CO₂ is a greenhouse gas, makes mildly acidic rain (carbonic acid) but not the major acid-rain culprit.

options.option_text: Lavoisier, who named it 'oxygen' but didn't discover
Joseph Priestley, in 1774, by heating HgO
Dalton, who proposed the atomic theory

questions.explanation: Joseph PRIESTLEY (Britain) — isolated O₂ on 1 Aug 1774 by heating mercuric oxide (HgO) with sunlight focused by a lens. Earlier, Carl SCHEELE (Sweden) had isolated it (1772-73) but published later. Antoine LAVOISIER (France) — named it 'OXYGENE' (Greek = 'acid maker', wrongly thought all acids contain it), recognised its role in combustion + respiration → overthrew the phlogiston theory. Distractor 3 = Cavendish discovered hydrogen (1766). Distractor 4 = Dalton's atomic theory (1808).

questions.stem: Hydrogen sulphide (H₂S) gas has the characteristic smell of:
questions.explanation: H₂S — colourless gas, smells like ROTTEN EGGS. Highly toxic (more than HCN at high concentrations), but human nose is very sensitive (detects from <0.5 ppb). Olfactory FATIGUE — at high concentrations, sense of smell is paralysed (dangerous!) — can't detect anymore. Sources: anaerobic decay (sewers, marshes), volcanic gases, oil/gas wells (sour gas). Used in lab: Lassaigne's test for sulphur in organic compounds; sulphide precipitation in qualitative analysis. Distractor 1 = HCN (cyanide). Distractor 4 = phosphine PH₃ partly.
